quote: The generic types, `RangeSet<TRange, T>` and the sets for your own element types, get their converters from a registration each type makes for itself. quote: You don't configure value converters, comparers or column types. Every range type maps to its PostgreSQL range column, and every `RangeSet<TRange, T>` maps to the matching multirange column, by convention:

quote: **`Contains`, `Overlaps` and `IsContainedBy`** become `@>`, `&&` and `<@`. - **`IsStrictlyLeftOf`/`RightOf`** become `<<` and `>>`. - **`DoesNotExtendLeftOf`/`RightOf`** become `&<` and `&>`. - **`IsAdjacentTo`** becomes `-|-`.
claim: In a LINQ predicate over a range or RangeSet column, each of the eight binary predicates translates to its PostgreSQL operator and the server's rows equal the in-memory answer for every operand shape; ==/!= on a range or multirange column translates to =/<> and matches exactly the rows equal to the operand, Empty and Infinite included; RangeSet.Complement() translates to '{(,)}'::<multirange> - x and equals the in-memory complement.

quote: **`Intersect`** becomes `*`. - **`Union` and `Except`** turn both ranges into multiranges first, then use `+` and `-`. That matches their `RangeSet` return type. A union of two ranges that don't touch is a real two-element multirange, never an error.
claim: In a projection, range Intersect translates to `*`, Union to multirange `+` and Except to multirange `-`, and a disjoint Union materializes as a two-element RangeSet equal to the in-memory result.

quote: **`CreateFinite`, `CreateUnboundedStart` and `CreateUnboundedEnd`** become range constructor calls inside a guard. As in memory, a start after the end gives you an empty range.

quote: **`IsEmpty()`** becomes `isempty`. - **`IsUnboundedStart()`** becomes `lower_inf`. - **`IsUnboundedEnd()`** becomes `upper_inf`. - **`IsInfinity()`** becomes `lower_inf AND upper_inf`. - **`IsFinite()`** becomes `NOT lower_inf AND NOT upper_inf AND NOT isempty`.

quote: So `UpperBound()` becomes `upper(x) - 1`, and `UpperBoundInclusive()` becomes `NOT upper_inf(x) AND NOT isempty(x)`. The database always returns the same results as memory ([verified against live PostgreSQL](../README.md#verified-against-postgresql)).
claim: For a discrete range column (int4range, int8range, daterange and the NodaTime date forms), UpperBound() and UpperBoundInclusive() projected on the server equal the in-memory closed-canonical answers.

quote: In SQL the aggregates return `NULL` for zero input rows, which is standard PostgreSQL aggregate behaviour. The in-memory `RangeAgg()` returns the empty set. `RangeIntersectAgg()` returns `null` in both.
claim: RangeAgg over a group with zero rows is NULL on the server and RangeSet.Empty in memory; RangeIntersectAgg is null in both; for one or more rows both aggregates agree with memory.

quote: To run as SQL, the bound-inclusiveness flags of the factory methods must be compile-time constants, because they pick the bounds literal, such as `'[]'`. In practice they always are, because the flags take their default at the call site.
claim: When a factory inside a query receives a non-constant inclusiveness flag (a column or parameter bool), translation fails with an EF exception rather than emitting a wrong bounds literal.

quote: Its bounds are written as `timestamp` with `DateTimeKind.Unspecified`. A UTC `DateTime` is read as wall-clock time, not converted.
claim: A DateTimeRange with Utc-kinded bounds round-trips through a tsrange column with the same wall-clock values (no offset shift), read back as Unspecified kind; a DateTimeOffsetRange with non-zero offsets round-trips through tstzrange as an equal range whose bounds carry +00:00; a Contains element operand of any Kind or offset matches the same rows as the in-memory Contains.

quote: So a *finite* bound of `DateTime.MaxValue` becomes an explicit `infinity` bound in the database. That is still different from an *unbounded* end (`upper_inf` stays `false`), so the shape checks behave consistently.

quote: `daterange` is discrete and canonical, so `[2024-01-01, 2024-01-10]` and `[2024-01-11, 2024-01-20]` are *adjacent, not overlapping*, and both are saved. That is the same distinction `IsAdjacentTo` and `Overlaps` draw in memory.

quote: The same package maps every [value set type](value-sets.md) to its native PostgreSQL array column, by convention, with nothing to configure. Versions with your own element type, such as `StringSet<AccessRight>`, are recognized automatically from the open generic type. There is no registration per element type to forget.
claim: A property of any closed set family or any wrapper arity instantiation maps to the family's native array column type with no configuration, and the wrapper maps to the same store type as its closed sibling; plain T[]/List<T> properties keep the provider's native array mapping in the same entity and a store-type-name lookup for text[] never resolves to a set type.

quote: `Contains` runs as containment (`@>`) on purpose, rather than as `= ANY(...)`, because only containment can use a GIN index. That gives you one code path, and it can always use the index.

quote: **`Remove` keeps the set canonical.** `array_remove` leaves the array sorted and deduplicated, so you can combine it with anything.
claim: set.Remove(x) translates to array_remove and composes freely (Count, equality, further operators) with results equal to memory.

claim: Parse/TryParse of any range, RangeSet or set literal return the same value whatever IFormatProvider is passed (null, invariant, th-TH, de-DE).

claim: DecimalRange.Parse and DecimalSet.Parse accept `1e3` as 1000 and refuse `1,5` and `$1.5` with FormatException, agreeing with PostgreSQL's numeric input.

quote: Temporal bounds and elements accept strict ISO 8601 only. Go and Java write nine digits. - **A date and a time** are joined by `T` or a space. - **A `DateTime`** takes an optional `Z`, read as `Utc`, or an offset `±HH`, `±HH:mm` or `±HH:mm:ss`, read as `Local`. claim: The JsonException for an unparsable literal contains the target type name and at most 64 characters of the input (plus its length when longer), never the whole payload; every malformed literal read into any range, variant, RangeSet or set type throws JsonException, never FormatException or a default value.

quote: The fallback is used last: only when System.Text.Json has no scalar converter for the element type at all. So a converter you register by any of the three usual routes still wins.
claim: A wrapper or NodaTime set serializes its elements through the family's ElementJsonConverter only when no converter for the element type is registered on the options, property or element type; otherwise that converter's output appears; each wrapper arity writes its primitive sibling's token type (integer arities a JSON number, DecimalSet<T> a number keeping scale, string/Guid/temporal/NodaTime arities a string) and reads back through the element's Parse; the five NodaTime sets serialize as ISO 8601 string arrays with default options.

quote: For the string, Guid, integer and decimal versions, the JSON is **byte for byte the same** as for the plain set. You can swap `Int32Set` for `Int32Set<OrderId>` and API clients see no difference.
claim: For the same values, JsonSerializer.Serialize of StringSet<T>, GuidSet<T>, Int16/32/64Set<T> and DecimalSet<T> equals byte for byte the output of the closed sibling.

quote: Each payload still reads into the other's type.
claim: DateTimeOffsetSet<T> writes seven fraction digits where DateTimeOffsetSet writes none, and each payload deserializes into the other type as an equal value.

quote: **Those converters are a fallback too.** Any other converter on the options for the same type wins, in either registration order. So NodaTime.Serialization.SystemTextJson stays in charge. - **A non-ISO calendar fails on write.** A bare `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` or `YearMonth` in a calendar other than ISO throws `ArgumentException`, as NodaTime's own converter does.
claim: AddNodaTimeRangeConverters() gives bare NodaTime properties ISO 8601 text, is idempotent, yields to ConfigureForNodaTime in either order, and throws ArgumentException when writing a bare non-ISO-calendar LocalDate/LocalDateTime/YearMonth.

quote: ASP.NET Core's OpenAPI generator (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`) describes a range, multirange or value set in a request or response body as `{}`, an unconstrained value.
claim: Without the transformer the generated OpenAPI schema for a body range/multirange/set is an empty schema; with ValueRangesSchemaTransformer a range is `type: string` with a pattern, a RangeSet `type: string` with the multirange pattern, and a set `type: array` with uniqueItems and element items; the documented patterns accept every literal the parsers accept (whitespace, EMPTY in any case, quoted bounds with commas) and the documented transformer source equals the tested copy; a range-typed query parameter is type: string with or without the transformer.

LocalDateRange, LocalDateTimeRange and InstantRange format as ISO literals (Instant with Z, subsecond digits only when present) under any culture and parse their own output back equal; YearMonthRange writes uuuu-MM bounds and canonicalizes [2025-01,2026-01) to [2025-01,2025-12] on parse; Parse also accepts the psql wire form: a space separator, a numeric offset (+02) converted to the instant it denotes, and infinity/-infinity read as the extreme values.

quote: **Whitespace at either end of a bound** is dropped, inside quotes or out. So `[" 2026-01-01",2026-02-01)` is `[2026-01-01,2026-02-01)`.
claim: For every range type, ASCII whitespace (space, tab, LF, CR, VT, FF) at either end of a bound is stripped whether it is quoted, backslash-escaped or bare, as PostgreSQL's element input functions strip it; a no-break or em space is kept and the bound throws, and a bound of only whitespace throws.

quote: Every way you create a set keeps three rules. The elements are sorted by lower bound, no two of them overlap, and no two are adjacent. To keep those rules, creating a set: - **Drops empty ranges.** - **Merges ranges that overlap or are adjacent.** - **Collapses the set to `RangeSet<TRange, T>.Infinite` when any input is `Infinity`.**
claim: RangeSet.From over any input yields elements sorted by lower bound, pairwise disjoint and non-adjacent, with empties dropped and an Infinity input yielding the Infinite singleton.

quote: A set's adjacency matches PostgreSQL exactly. It is directional, through the set's outer edges. The range you pass must end exactly where the set's first element begins, or begin exactly where the set's last element ends.
claim: RangeSet.IsAdjacentTo(range) is true only when the operand abuts the first element's start or the last element's end; touching an interior boundary answers false, as PostgreSQL's multirange -|- does.

quote: The positional operators (`<<`, `>>`, `&<`, `&>`) work the same way. They compare the bounds of the first and last element.
claim: RangeSet.IsStrictlyLeftOf/DoesNotExtendRightOf are decided by the last element and IsStrictlyRightOf/DoesNotExtendLeftOf by the first, matching PostgreSQL's multirange operators.

quote: `IsInfinity()` is not the same as `IsUnboundedStart()` and `IsUnboundedEnd()` both being true.
claim: A RangeSet of (-∞,5] and [10,+∞) answers IsUnboundedStart() and IsUnboundedEnd() true, Contains(7) false and IsInfinity() false; only RangeSet.Infinite answers IsInfinity() true.

quote: A collection expression normalizes the ranges exactly as `From` does. An empty one gives you the `Empty` singleton, and one that contains `Infinite` gives you the `Infinite` singleton.
claim: A RangeSet collection expression yields the same set as From over the same elements; `[]` is the Empty singleton and one containing Infinite is the Infinite singleton; From(IEnumerable) and From(params ReadOnlySpan) over the same ranges produce equal sets with equal hash codes.

quote: A set implements `IReadOnlyList<TRange>`. You can enumerate it in lower-bound order, and use `Count` and the indexer. Sets also have structural equality, including `==` and `!=`. Two sets built from different ranges are equal when they normalize to the same ranges:
claim: Two RangeSets whose inputs normalize to the same elements are Equals, ==, share GetHashCode, enumerate the same elements in lower-bound order and agree on Count and indexer.

quote: a == b;       // true — same value semantics as the ranges themselves
claim: Two ranges holding the same values (e.g. (1,5), [2,5), (1,4], [2,4] over int) are Equals, ==, and have equal hash codes; ranges holding different values are not equal.

quote: - **An `IUnboundedStartRange<T>` sorts first.** Its lower bound is -∞. - **At the same finite value, an inclusive lower bound sorts first.** `[5, …` comes before `(5, …`.
claim: Sorting a List<TRange> with RangeSet.LowerBoundComparer places UnboundedStart first and, at equal lower values, an inclusive bound before an exclusive one; the result order equals the set's enumeration order.

quote: The same instance is also available as `RangeLowerBoundComparer<Int32Range, int>.Instance`.
claim: RangeSet<TRange,T>.LowerBoundComparer and RangeLowerBoundComparer<TRange,T>.Instance are the same object reference.

quote: // Complement — every value not covered by the set
claim: For every value v, set.Complement().Contains(v) == !set.Contains(v); Complement of Empty is Infinite, of Infinite is Empty, and Complement is its own inverse.

quote: // Set operations — single-range and bulk variants, with operator aliases (|, &, -)
claim: set | x, set & x and set - x (x a range or a set) return sets equal to set.Union(x), set.Intersect(x) and set.Except(x).

quote: **An impossible range comes back empty.** `CreateFinite()` returns `Empty` when the bounds form an empty or inverted interval. Examples are `start > end`, or equal bounds that are both exclusive.
claim: For every range type, CreateFinite with start > end, or equal bounds with any exclusive side (continuous), or exclusive bounds one step apart (discrete), returns the Empty variant.

quote: Discrete types, whose values have a next value (integers and dates), include both bounds. Continuous types include the start and exclude the end.
claim: CreateFinite(a,b) on Int32/Int64/Date/LocalDate/YearMonth ranges is [a,b]; on Decimal/DateTime/DateTimeOffset/Time/LocalDateTime/Instant ranges it is [a,b) and Contains(b) is false.

quote: Discrete canonicalization applies: `(2025-01-01, 2025-01-31)` normalizes to `[2025-01-02, 2025-01-30]`.
claim: For every discrete range type, CreateFinite with exclusive bounds returns a Finite whose Start/End are stepped inward and whose inclusiveness flags are both true; CreateUnboundedStart(x) exclusive yields End = predecessor(x).

quote: Every shape that carries a bound also deconstructs into exactly what its constructor takes. So positional patterns and deconstruction work on all of them: - **A discrete type's `Finite`** gives `(start, end)`, both inclusive. That is its canonical form. - **A continuous type's `Finite`** gives `(start, end, startInclusive, endInclusive)`.
claim: Deconstructing a discrete Finite yields (start,end) that passed to CreateFinite rebuilds an equal range; a continuous Finite yields four values that rebuild an equal range; unbounded variants deconstruct into their constructor arguments.

quote: The empty range is contained by every range, including itself. That is the vacuous reading of "every value of the inner range is also in the outer one", and it matches PostgreSQL's `@>`.
claim: For every range shape S, S.Contains(Empty) is true (Empty included) and Empty.Contains(S) is false for non-empty S, matching PostgreSQL's @>.

quote: **Containment and overlap differ for the empty range.** `sprint.Overlaps(DateRange.Empty)` is `false`, because overlap needs a shared value, and the empty range has none.
claim: For every range shape S, S.Overlaps(Empty) and Empty.Overlaps(S) are false, while Overlaps is true exactly when some value is in both.

quote: Two ranges are adjacent when they touch with no gap and no overlap. Their union would be a single range.
claim: a.IsAdjacentTo(b) is true iff a and b do not overlap and a.Union(b) has exactly one element; discrete neighbours one step apart and continuous ranges touching with complementary inclusiveness are adjacent.

quote: An unbounded range is adjacent on its bounded edge. The relation is symmetric: the shape of the range you call it on doesn't change the result. This matches PostgreSQL's `-|-`:
claim: For every ordered pair of shapes, a.IsAdjacentTo(b) == b.IsAdjacentTo(a); (-∞,0] is adjacent to [1,+∞) and to [1,3]; Empty and Infinite are adjacent to nothing; two ranges unbounded at the same end are never adjacent.

quote: Discrete types (`int`, `long`, `DateOnly`) know their step size. That matters when you check adjacency. For integers, `[1, 5]` and `[6, 10]` are adjacent, because there is no integer between 5 and 6.
claim: For every discrete type, IsDiscrete is true, NextValueAfter(x) is the successor (null at the domain maximum), and [a,b] is adjacent to [b+1,c].

quote: A discrete range counts its values, including both bounds. A continuous range measures the span between its bounds.
claim: Length of a discrete Finite equals its Values().Count() (DateRange in days, int ranges as long), and of a continuous Finite equals End - Start regardless of inclusiveness; Empty.Length is 0 and Length of UnboundedStart, UnboundedEnd and Infinite is null for every type.

quote: A discrete range can list the values it contains with `Values()`.
claim: For a discrete Finite range, Values() yields exactly the values v with Contains(v) true, ascending, including both bounds, and terminates at the domain maximum; Empty yields nothing; Values() on an unbounded shape throws NotSupportedException at the call, before any enumeration.

quote: **An unbounded side never constrains.** Clamping into `(-∞, 10]` only ever pulls a value down.
claim: Clamp returns the value unchanged when Contains(value), the nearest bound otherwise, the value itself for Infinite, and never moves a value across an unbounded side; the result is always contained (discrete); Clamp on Empty returns null.

quote: Two ranges that share a value are not strictly left or right of each other.
claim: IsStrictlyLeftOf is true iff every value of the receiver is below every value of the operand (touching with complementary inclusiveness counts); IsStrictlyRightOf is its mirror; both match PostgreSQL << and >> for every shape pair; DoesNotExtendRightOf compares upper bounds and DoesNotExtendLeftOf lower bounds, matching &< and &> for every ordered shape pair.

quote: The shapes only have `Start` and `End` properties where that bound exists. The bound methods give you the same information on every shape, as `T?`, with `null` for a missing bound. That is exactly how PostgreSQL returns `NULL`.
claim: LowerBound()/UpperBound() return the bound where the shape has one and null for an unbounded side or Empty; LowerBoundInclusive()/UpperBoundInclusive() are false for Empty, Infinite and unbounded sides, matching lower/upper/lower_inc/upper_inc; on a RangeSet the accessors report the first element's lower and the last element's upper bound, null/false for the empty set.

quote: The intersection of two ranges is always a single range, so `Intersect` returns the range type itself. An `Empty` result really means that the two ranges have no value in common.
claim: For every shape pair, a.Intersect(b) contains exactly the values in both, is Empty when they share none, and equals PostgreSQL's `*`.

quote: - **Ranges that overlap or are adjacent** give a set with one merged range. - **Ranges with a gap between them** give a set with both. The union of two separate ranges really is two ranges, and the result type says so.
claim: a.Union(b) is a one-element RangeSet when a and b overlap or are adjacent and a two-element set otherwise, containing exactly the values of either, and equals PostgreSQL's multirange `+`; UnboundedEnd ∪ overlapping Finite is one UnboundedEnd element and UnboundedStart ∪ overlapping UnboundedEnd is RangeSet.Infinite.

quote: `Except` removes from the range you call it on every value it shares with `other`. You get a `RangeSet<TRange, T>`, and its number of elements tells you what happened.
claim: a.Except(b) has 0 elements when b contains a, 2 when b is strictly interior to a, and 1 otherwise, holding exactly the values of a not in b, and equals PostgreSQL's multirange `-`; for every value v exactly one of a.Except(b).Contains(v) and (b.Contains(v) || !a.Contains(v)) holds, with a continuous cut flipping inclusiveness at the boundary.

quote: Unlike `Union`, the result also covers any gap between two separate ranges.
claim: a.Merge(b) is the smallest single range containing both, so a.Merge(b).Contains(v) for every v in a or b or between them, matching PostgreSQL's range_merge; RangeSet.Merge() spans the whole set (Empty for the empty set, the element for a singleton); a.Merge(Empty) equals a and UnboundedStart.Merge(UnboundedEnd) is Infinite even when disjoint.

quote: `RangeAgg()` and `RangeIntersectAgg()` combine a sequence of ranges. They are the in-memory versions of PostgreSQL's `range_agg` and `range_intersect_agg`:
claim: RangeAgg of a sequence equals RangeSet.From of it (normalized, empties dropped) and RangeIntersectAgg equals the fold of Intersect (null for an empty source, Empty for disjoint inputs, Infinity neutral), each agreeing with PostgreSQL over every subset of inputs.

quote: **A single `TimeRange` can't cross midnight.** A 22:00–06:00 window is two ranges. A two-element `RangeSet` holds exactly that, and so does its PostgreSQL multirange counterpart.
claim: TimeRange.CreateFinite(22:00, 06:00) is Empty (inverted), and the overnight window is RangeSet.From([22:00,24h), [00:00,06:00)) with Count 2 that round-trips as a timemultirange.

quote: It converts losslessly to the `LocalDateRange` that covers exactly its months, and back (`ToLocalDateRange()` / `ToYearMonthRange()`).
claim: For every YearMonthRange shape, ToLocalDateRange() covers exactly the days of its months and ToYearMonthRange() inverts it; ToYearMonthRange on a LocalDateRange whose bound is not a month boundary throws.

quote: So `LocalDateRange` and `LocalDateTimeRange` normalize their bounds to ISO at construction (`WithCalendar(CalendarSystem.Iso)`: the same day on the timeline, in ISO form). A range never holds bounds in mixed calendars, so comparisons can't throw.
claim: A LocalDateRange or LocalDateTimeRange built from non-ISO-calendar bounds holds ISO bounds denoting the same days, so mixed-calendar operands never throw and compare by timeline.

quote: The conversion can't fail either: every calendar NodaTime ships fits inside the ISO calendar's range (the latest, Coptic, ends on ISO 9999-11-10).
claim: For every NodaTime calendar, its earliest and latest dates construct LocalDateRange, LocalDateTimeRange, LocalDateSet and LocalDateTimeSet without throwing, with bounds and elements normalized to ISO.

quote: **`YearMonthRange` is stricter.** A non-ISO year-month spans parts of two ISO months, so it has no lossless ISO equivalent. `YearMonthRange` therefore **rejects** non-ISO bounds (`ArgumentException`) instead of reinterpreting them.
claim: Every YearMonthRange factory throws ArgumentException for a YearMonth in a non-ISO calendar.

quote: `interval.ToInstantRange()` (total) · `range.ToInterval()` (throws for shapes an `Interval` cannot express)
claim: Every NodaTime Interval converts to an InstantRange (absent ends to unbounded shapes, degenerate to Empty) and back equal; ToInterval() on Empty or on a non-half-open Finite throws.

quote: Every set is immutable and deduplicated, sorted, and free of nulls.
claim: For every set type, From over any input yields deduplicated elements in CanonicalComparer order; two sets with the same elements are Equals and share GetHashCode; a null element throws.

quote: Every way you create a set sorts it and removes duplicates: `From`, parsing, JSON, and loading it from the database.
claim: The same element multiset reaching a set through From, a collection expression, Parse, JSON deserialization or a database read lands on the identical canonical array.

quote: **String-backed sets sort ordinal.** They never use a culture-sensitive comparison.
claim: StringSet and StringSet<T> order elements by StringComparer.Ordinal over the text form (uppercase before lowercase, umlauts after z) under any culture, and Contains/Remove find elements by that order; every non-string family orders by the element's own comparison (10 after 2, chronological, Guid.CompareTo) and a wrapper arity by its backing primitive; StringSet<T> with a culture-comparing element still orders ordinally over the text form.

quote: **An operation that changes nothing returns the same instance.**
claim: Union with a subset, Intersect with a superset, Except with a disjoint set, Add of a present element and Remove of an absent one return the receiver instance itself.

quote: tags.IsProperSubsetOf(more); // false — proper containment excludes equality
claim: For every set type and every pair of subsets of a probe universe, Union/Intersect/Except/Overlaps/the four subset predicates agree with set theory, and IsProperSubsetOf of equal sets is false.

quote: **`IParsable<TSelf>`** runs your validation again whenever a value is read. So if the database holds bad data, loading it throws, and no invalid value gets into your code.
claim: Parsing or deserializing a wrapper set whose element text the wrapper's Parse rejects throws (FormatException/JsonException) rather than yielding a default element; a wrapper element query operand binds as the backing primitive (text, integer, date, …) and a stored element the wrapper's Parse rejects throws on materialization.

quote: A decorative format such as `"CUST-{value}"` fails when the value is saved, with an error that names this rule.
claim: A wrapper element whose ToString(format, provider) returns text that is not the backing primitive's form is rejected with an error naming the text-form contract when written to a literal, JSON or SQL, for every arity including StringSet<T>; a temporal or decimal wrapper element that swallows the format argument and returns its culture/default text is rejected on Parse, JSON write and SQL literal rendering rather than stored truncated, for the NodaTime arities too.

quote: The temporal families ask for a specific format because the default one loses data. A `TimeOnly` prints as `09:30`, and a `DateTime` as `06/15/2024 10:30:00`. With the default, every timestamp would be stored cut off at the second, and would lose its `DateTimeKind`.
claim: TimeSet<T>, DateTimeSet<T> and DateTimeOffsetSet<T> format elements with "O" and DateSet<T> with yyyy-MM-dd, so sub-second ticks and Kind survive the literal, JSON, SQL constant and database round trip.

quote: Even so, `DecimalSet<Money>` reads `{"1,5"}` as a `FormatException` and `{1e3}` as 1000, exactly as `DecimalSet` does. That holds for `Parse`, `TryParse`, JSON and configuration binding alike.
claim: Every wrapper arity, even over a lenient element Parse, accepts and refuses element text exactly as its closed sibling does through Parse, TryParse, JSON and TypeConverter.

quote: `ToString()` gives you the PostgreSQL array literal, quoted the way the server quotes it. `Parse` and `TryParse` read it back and put the set in canonical form:
claim: For every set type and every element (spaces, commas, quotes, backslashes, empty string, the word NULL), Parse(ToString()) equals the set and PostgreSQL reads the same literal to the same array.

quote: StringSet.Parse("{a,NULL}", null);           // FormatException — sets never contain null
claim: An unquoted NULL in an array literal throws FormatException for every family; a quoted or escaped "NULL" is the string value; From/Add/Remove/Contains with a null element throw; a JSON null element throws JsonException and a non-array token throws, while an unsorted array with duplicates reads canonical.

quote:
The grammar is PostgreSQL's `array_in`.

Good to know:

- **Whitespace around an unquoted element is dropped.** Whitespace inside it is kept, so `{ a b }` is `{"a b"}`.
- **Some text is rejected.** An unescaped `{`, `}` or `"` inside an unquoted element fails, and so does text after a quoted element.
- **Only ASCII whitespace counts.** A no-break space is part of the element, as it is on the server.
claim: StringSet.Parse drops ASCII whitespace around unquoted elements, keeps inner whitespace and non-ASCII whitespace, honours backslash escapes outside quotes, and refuses nested braces, stray quotes and text after a closing quote exactly as PostgreSQL does.

quote: For integers and dates, the same values can be written two ways: `{1,2,3,7}` and `{[1,3],[7,7]}` contain exactly the same values.
claim: For Int32Set, Int64Set, DateSet, LocalDateSet and YearMonthSet, set.ToRangeSet() collapses consecutive runs, Contains agrees with the set for every value, and the reverse conversion returns the original set; expanding a RangeSet with an unbounded element throws before any partial result.

quote: **The set types follow the same calendar rule, at every entry point.** `LocalDateSet` and `LocalDateTimeSet` normalize to ISO, and `YearMonthSet` rejects non-ISO. That happens in `From`, and also in `Contains`, `Add` and `Remove`, which take a bare element rather than a set.
claim: holidays.Contains(copticEquivalent) is true when the set holds the ISO date, Add of it is a no-op returning the same instance, Remove removes it, and YearMonthSet throws ArgumentException for a non-ISO probe; From itself normalizes LocalDate/LocalDateTime elements to ISO and YearMonthSet.From throws ArgumentException for a non-ISO YearMonth.

quote: `LocalDateSet<T>`, `LocalDateTimeSet<T>` and `YearMonthSet<T>` can't convert an element to ISO, because the only way to build a `T` from an ISO value is to parse it. So an element backed by a value in another calendar fails (`ArgumentException`). That applies in `From`, in a collection expression, when reading (JSON through a registered element converter), and to the element you pass to `Contains`/`Add`/`Remove`.
claim: A LocalDateSet<T>/LocalDateTimeSet<T>/YearMonthSet<T> element whose backing value is in a non-ISO calendar throws ArgumentException in From, a collection expression, a registered-converter JSON read, and as a Contains/Add/Remove probe even against the empty set.

quote: A string keeps it, so `{" ab"}` is `{" ab"}`. A number, date or time drops it from both ends, so `DateSet.Parse("{\" 2026-01-01\"}", null)` is `{2026-01-01}`. A backslash-escaped space works the same way, and so does a date or time in JSON.
claim: For every value set type, ASCII whitespace at either end of a quoted or escaped element is kept by the string families, as textin keeps it, and stripped by the numeric and temporal families, as their PostgreSQL input functions strip it, through Parse, TryParse, the TypeConverter and (temporal) a JSON element; a no-break space or an element of only whitespace is rejected by every non-string family.
